      <content name="title">Childhood Brain Tumors</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Brain tumors are abnormal growths inside the skull. They are among the most common types of childhood cancers. Some are benign tumors, which aren't cancer. They can still be serious. Malignant tumors are cancerous.</p><p>Childhood brain and spinal cord tumors can cause headaches and other symptoms. However, other conditions can also cause the same symptoms. Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following problems:</p><ul><li>Morning headache or headache that goes away after vomiting</li><li>Frequent nausea and vomiting</li><li>Vision, hearing, and speech problems</li><li>Loss of balance or trouble walking</li><li>Unusual sleepiness</li><li>Personality changes</li><li>Seizures</li><li>Increased head size in infants</li></ul><p>The symptoms are not the same in every child.</p><p>Doctors use physical and neurological exams, lab tests, and imaging to diagnose brain tumors. Most childhood brain tumors are diagnosed and removed in surgery.</p><p>Treatment for children is sometimes different than for an adult. Long-term side effects are an important issue. The options also depend on the type of tumor and where it is. Removal of the tumor is often possible. If not, radiation, chemotherapy, or both may be used.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/acutelymphocyticleukemia.html">
      <content name="title">Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ALL</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Leukemia, Acute Lymphoblastic</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Leukemia, Acute Lymphocytic</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is leukemia?<p>Leukemia is a term for cancers of the blood cells. Leukemia starts in blood-forming tissues such as the bone marrow. Your bone marrow makes the cells which will develop into white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. Each type of cell has a different job:</p><ul><li>White blood cells help your body fight infection</li><li>Red blood cells deliver oxygen from your lungs to your tissues and organs</li><li>Platelets help form clots to stop bleeding</li></ul><p>When you have leukemia, your bone marrow makes large numbers of abnormal cells. This problem most often happens with white blood cells. These abnormal cells build up in your bone marrow and blood. They crowd out the healthy blood cells and make it hard for your cells and blood to do their work.</p>What is acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>Acute lymphocytic leukemia is a type of acute leukemia. It's also called ALL and acute lymphoblastic leukemia. "Acute" means that it usually gets worse quickly if it's not treated. ALL is the most common type of cancer in children. It can also affect adults.</p><p>In ALL, the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. These cells normally help your body fight infection. But in ALL, they are abnormal and cannot fight infection very well. They also crowd out the healthy cells, which can lead to infection, anemia, and easy bleeding. These abnormal cells can also spread to other parts of the body, including the brain and spinal cord.</p>What causes acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>ALL happens when there are changes in the genetic material (DNA) in bone marrow cells. The cause of these genetic changes is unknown. However, there are certain factors that raise your risk of ALL.</p>Who is at risk for acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>The factors that raise your risk of ALL include:</p><ul><li>Being male</li><li>Being white</li><li>Being over age 70</li><li>Having had chemotherapy or radiation therapy</li><li>Having been exposed to high levels of radiation</li><li>Having certain genetic disorders, such as Down syndrome</li></ul>What are the symptoms of acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>The signs and symptoms of ALL include:</p><ul><li>Weakness or feeling tired</li><li>Fever or night sweats</li><li>Easy bruising or bleeding</li><li>Petechiae, which are tiny red dots under the skin. They are caused by bleeding.</li><li>Shortness of breath</li><li>Weight loss or loss of appetite</li><li>Pain in the bones or stomach</li><li>Pain or feeling of fullness below the ribs</li><li>Swollen lymph nodes - you may notice them as painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin</li><li>Having had many infections</li></ul>How is acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to diagnose ALL and figure out which subtype you have:</p><ul><li>A physical exam</li><li>A medical history</li><li>Blood tests, such as
      <ul><li>Complete blood count (CBC) with differential</li><li>Blood chemistry tests such as a basic metabolic panel (BMP), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), kidney function tests, liver function tests, and electrolyte panel</li><li>Blood smear</li></ul>  
</li><li>Bone marrow tests. There are two main types - bone marrow aspiration and bone marrow biopsy. Both tests involve removing a sample of bone marrow and bone. The samples are sent to a lab for testing.</li><li>Genetic tests to look for gene and chromosome changes</li></ul><p>If you are diagnosed with ALL, you may have additional tests to see whether the cancer has spread. These include imaging tests and a lumbar puncture, which is a procedure to collect and test <span class="qt0">cerebrospinal</span> fluid (CSF).</p>What are the treatments for acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>Treatments for ALL include:</p><ul><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy with stem cell transplant</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific cancer cells with less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>Treatment is usually done in two phases:</p><ul><li>The goal of the first phase is to kill the leukemia cells in the blood and bone marrow. This treatment puts the leukemia into remission. Remission means that the signs and symptoms of cancer are reduced or have disappeared.</li><li>The second phase is known as post-remission therapy. Its goal is to prevent a relapse (return) of the cancer. It involves killing any remaining leukemia cells that may not be active but could begin to regrow.</li></ul><p>Treatment during both phases also usually includes <span class="qt2">central nervous system</span> (CNS) prophylaxis therapy. This therapy helps prevent the spread of leukemia cells to the brain and spinal cord. It may be high dose chemotherapy or chemotherapy injected into the spinal cord. It also sometimes includes radiation therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/alcohol.html">
      <content name="title">Alcohol</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alcohol Consumption</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Binge Drinking</content>
      <content name="altTitle">College Drinking</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Drinking</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Many Americans drink alcohol at least occasionally. The  Dietary Guidelines for Americans say that adults of legal drinking age should either not drink or drink in moderation. Drinking less is better for your health than drinking more. Also, there are some people who should not drink at all.</p><p>If you are going to drink, it's important to know how alcohol affects you and how much is too much.</p>How does alcohol affect the body?<p>Alcohol is a <span class="qt2">central nervous system</span> depressant. This means that it is a drug that slows down brain activity. It can change your mood, behavior, and self-control. It can cause problems with memory and thinking clearly. Alcohol can also affect your coordination and physical control.</p><p>Alcohol also has effects on the other organs in your body. For example, it can raise your blood pressure and heart rate. If you drink too much at once, it could make you throw up.</p>Why are the effects of alcohol different from person to person?<p>Alcohol's effects vary from person to person, depending on a variety of factors, including:</p><ul><li>How much you drink</li><li>How often you drink</li><li>Your age</li><li>Your sex</li><li>Your genetics</li><li>Your overall health</li><li>Whether or not you have a family history of alcohol problems</li></ul>What is moderate drinking?<ul><li>For most women, moderate drinking is no more than 1 standard drink a day</li><li>For most men, moderate drinking is no more than 2 standard drinks a day</li></ul><p>Even though moderate drinking may be safe for many people, there are still risks. Moderate drinking can raise the risk of death from certain cancers and heart diseases.</p>What is a standard drink?<p>In the United States, a standard drink is one that contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which is found in:</p><ul><li>12 ounces of regular beer (5% alcohol content)</li><li>5 ounces of wine (12% alcohol content)</li><li>1.5 ounces or a "shot" of distilled spirits or liquor (40% alcohol content)</li></ul>Who should not drink alcohol?<p>Some people should not drink alcohol at all, including those who:</p><ul><li>Are in recovery from an alcohol use disorder (AUD)</li><li> Are unable to control the amount they drink</li><li>Are under age 21</li><li>Are pregnant or trying to become pregnant</li><li>Are taking medicines that can interact with alcohol</li><li>Have medical conditions that can get worse if you drink alcohol</li><li>Are planning on driving</li><li>Will be operating machinery or doing activities that require skill, coordination, and alertness</li></ul><p>If you have questions about whether it is safe for you to drink, talk with your health care provider.</p>What is excessive drinking?<p>Excessive drinking includes binge drinking and heavy alcohol use:</p><ul><li>Binge drinking is drinking so much at once that your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) level is 0.08% or more: 
  <ul><li>For men, this usually happens after having 5 or more drinks within a few hours.</li><li>For women, it is usually after about 4 or more drinks within a few hours.</li></ul>
</li><li>Heavy alcohol use means:
  <ul><li>For men, having more than 5 drinks on any day or more than 15 drinks per week.</li><li>For women, having more than 4 drinks on any day or more than 8 drinks per week.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Binge drinking raises your risk of injuries, car crashes, and alcohol overdose. It also puts you at risk of becoming violent or being the victim of violence.</p><p>Heavy alcohol use over a long period of time may cause health problems such as:</p><ul><li>Alcohol use disorder (AUD)</li><li>Liver diseases, including cirrhosis and alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD)</li><li>Heart diseases</li><li>Increased risk of certain cancers</li><li>Increased risk of injuries</li></ul><p>Heavy alcohol use can also cause problems at home, at work, and with friends. But treatment can help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/braintumors.html">
      <content name="title">Brain Tumors</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Brain Cancer</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Glioma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Meningioma</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A brain tumor is a growth of abnormal cells in the tissues of the brain. Brain tumors can be benign, with no cancer cells, or malignant, with cancer cells that grow quickly.  Some are primary brain tumors, which start in the brain. Others are metastatic, and they start somewhere else in the body and move to the brain.</p><p>Brain tumors can cause many symptoms. Some of the most common are:</p><ul><li>Headaches, often in the morning </li><li>Nausea and vomiting</li><li>Changes in your ability to talk, hear, or see</li><li>Problems with balance or walking</li><li>Problems with thinking or memory </li><li>Feeling weak or sleepy</li><li>Changes in your mood or behavior</li><li>Seizures</li></ul><p>Doctors diagnose brain tumors by doing a neurologic exam and tests including an MRI, CT scan, and biopsy. Treatment options include watchful waiting, surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack cancer cells with less harm to normal cells. Many people get a combination of treatments.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/caffeine.html">
      <content name="title">Caffeine</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Energy Drinks</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is caffeine?<p>Caffeine is a bitter substance that occurs naturally in more than 60 plants including:</p><ul><li>Coffee beans</li><li>Tea leaves</li><li>Kola nuts, which are used to flavor soft drink colas</li><li>Cacao pods, which are used to make chocolate products</li></ul><p>There is also synthetic (man-made) caffeine, which is added to some medicines, foods, and drinks. For example, some pain relievers, cold medicines, and over-the-counter medicines for alertness contain synthetic caffeine. So do energy drinks and "energy-boosting" gums and snacks.</p><p>Most people consume caffeine from drinks. The amount of caffeine in different drinks can vary a lot, but it is generally:</p><ul><li>An 8-ounce cup of coffee: 95-200 mg</li><li>A 12-ounce can of cola: 35-45 mg</li><li>An 8-ounce energy drink: 70-100 mg</li><li>An 8-ounce cup of tea: 14-60 mg</li></ul>What are caffeine's effects on the body?<p>Caffeine has many effects on your body's metabolism. It:</p><ul><li>Stimulates your <span class="qt2">central nervous system</span>, which can make you feel more awake and give you a boost of energy</li><li>Is a diuretic, meaning that it helps your body get rid of extra salt and water by urinating more</li><li>Increases the release of acid in your stomach, sometimes leading to an upset stomach or heartburn</li><li>May interfere with the absorption of calcium in the body</li><li>Increases your blood pressure</li></ul><p>Within one hour of eating or drinking caffeine, it reaches its peak level in your blood. You may continue to feel the effects of caffeine for four to six hours.</p>What are the side effects from too much caffeine?<p>For most people, it is not harmful to consume up to 400mg of caffeine a day. If you do eat or drink too much caffeine, it can cause health problems, such as:</p><ul><li>Restlessness and shakiness</li><li>Insomnia</li><li>Headaches</li><li>Dizziness</li><li>Fast heart rate</li><li>Dehydration</li><li>Anxiety</li><li>Dependency, so you need to take more of it to get the same results</li></ul><p>Some people are more sensitive to the effects of caffeine than others.</p>What are energy drinks, and why can they be a problem?<p>Energy drinks are beverages that have added caffeine. The amount of caffeine in energy drinks can vary widely, and sometimes the labels on the drinks do not give you the actual amount of caffeine in them. Energy drinks may also contain sugars, vitamins, herbs, and supplements.</p><p>Companies that make energy drinks claim that the drinks can increase alertness and improve physical and mental performance. This has helped make the drinks popular with American teens and young adults. There's limited data showing that energy drinks might temporarily improve alertness and physical endurance. There is not enough evidence to show that they enhance strength or power. But what we do know is that energy drinks can be dangerous because they have large amounts of caffeine. And since they have lots of sugar, they can contribute to weight gain and worsen diabetes.</p><p>Sometimes young people mix their energy drinks with alcohol. It is dangerous to combine alcohol and caffeine. Caffeine can interfere with your ability to recognize how drunk you are, which can lead you to drink more. This also makes you more likely to make bad decisions.</p>Who should avoid or limit caffeine?<p>You should check with your health care provider about whether you should limit or avoid caffeine if you:</p><ul><li>Are pregnant, since caffeine passes through the placenta to your baby.</li><li>Are breastfeeding, since a small amount of caffeine that you consume is passed along to your baby.</li><li>Have sleep disorders, including insomnia.</li><li>Have migraines or other chronic headaches.</li><li>Have anxiety.</li><li>Have GERD or ulcers.</li><li>Have arrhythmia (a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat).</li><li>Have high blood pressure.</li><li>Take certain medicines or supplements, including stimulants, certain antibiotics, asthma medicines, and heart medicines. Check with your health care provider about whether there might be interactions between caffeine and any medicines and supplements that you take.</li><li>Are a child or teen. Neither should have as much caffeine as adults. Children can be especially sensitive to the effects of caffeine.</li></ul>What is caffeine withdrawal?<p>If you have been consuming caffeine on a regular basis and then suddenly stop, you may have caffeine withdrawal. Symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Headaches</li><li>Drowsiness</li><li>Irritability</li><li>Nausea</li><li>Trouble concentrating</li></ul><p>These symptoms usually go away after a couple of days.</p></content>
